prompts.prompt_text:
1 week rota for my employees for 15th-21st December 2025, I have 2 FT (26-34 hour per week) and 4 PT employees (16-24 hours per week). Full-time employees are Maria and Nuria, part-time employees are Nate, Jack, Ben, and Finn. We are a bar closing at late times so the shifts are 16:00-22:00, 16:00-23:00, 18:00-01:00, 19:00-01:00, 1 person per shift for Thursday-Sunday inclusive. Monday-Tuesday shifts are 16:00-21:00, 16:00-23:00, 17:00-23:00. We are closed on Wednesdays. It's coming up to Christmas holiday season so I'm having trouble making this rota around my employees booked days off. Can you make this rota? 

Full-time employees are also senior staff, so I need at least one FTer to work the closing shift to cash-up every night we are open (the PTers aren't trained to do this). Also, Nate and Jack who joined us for this holiday period are both under-18 so they can't handle alcohol alone, don't schedule either of them unless there is at least one adult working at the same time. Maria has a family event on Friday, so don't schedule her any shifts that day, and on Sundays, she needs to finish before midnight because buses don't run late. Ben goes to university so can't do shifts starting at 16:00 on the weekdays, 17:00 and after is okay. 

Don't schedule FT staff to work more than 5 days in total, and PT shouldn't work more than 4 days in total, this is in their contracts. I want to be a good employer, so I want the PTers to have at least 2 consecutive days off (including our closed Wednesday), it would be annoying if they had to come in to work every other day. I need the total hours for each employee for this week to calculate payroll, FT are on £16.5 per hour, Nate and Jack who are only with us for this seasonal rush are on £14 per hour, Ben and Finn who are our regular PTers are on £14.5 per hour, sum up each employee's total hours at the end.

Right ok so I’m ta’ing for a class and we need to do some grade calculations and analysis. There are 30 students, 7 assignments each, all of them out of 25 points. So the category of assignments these are in will add up to 175 points but i also need the percentage for each student. And i want a per student breakdown but then also one that looks at each assignment for the class as a whole.
So first would be the per student breakdown so give me a list of all the students. I need their point total out of 175 first, then their percentage, then their letter grade based on this scale:
A+ = 97–100%
A = 93–96%
A− = 90–92%
B+ = 87–89%
B = 83–86%
B− = 80–82%
C+ = 77–79%
C = 73–76%
C− = 70–72%
D+ = 67–69%
D = 63–66%
D− = 60–62%
F = 0–59%
Then after that i need to know each student’s best assignment and worst assignment, and if they have multiple best/worst assignments, you can list them all. So like if someone scores 25 on assignments 4 and 7, you can list assignments 4 and 7 for their best assignments. List best first then worst.
Oh and make the student list alphabetical by last initial, write the point total in bold and like “167/175,” bold the percentage, and bold the letter grade. Put the letter grade in parentheses next to the percentage. don’t list them using bullets/numbers. And the student names should be bolded and capitalized.

So then for the second part, i want a breakdown by assignment, so for each assignment i need some stats. Tell me the average score of the assignment, in points and then in percentage with the letter grade in parentheses next to the percentage. If any students get a perfect score, list their names next, and same for if any students get a zero. Put the assignment name (e.g., “assignment #4”) in bold.

Oh and for the first part, the student breakdown, underneath everything you already listed, if any student has a 0 on an assignment, put a note saying so and specifying the assignment, like this: “*0 on assignment #_” so the prof knows to talk to them. If any student has a grade of C or below, also list a note that says “*low grade, professor to meet with student”

And then at the end of the second part, tell me which assignment has the best average score and which has the worst.

prompts.prompt_text:
1 week rota for my employees for 15th-21st December 2025, I have 2 FT (26-34 hour per week) and 4 PT employees (16-24 hours per week). Full-time employees are Maria and Nuria, part-time employees are Nate, Jack, Ben, and Finn. We are a bar closing at late times so the shifts are 16:00-22:00, 16:00-23:00, 18:00-01:00, 19:00-01:00, 1 person per shift for Thursday-Sunday inclusive. Monday-Tuesday shifts are 16:00-21:00, 16:00-23:00, 17:00-23:00. We are closed on Wednesdays. It's coming up to Christmas holiday season so I'm having trouble making this rota around my employees booked days off. Can you make this rota? 

Full-time employees are also senior staff, so I need at least one FTer to work the closing shift to cash-up every night we are open (the PTers aren't trained to do this). Also, Nate and Jack who joined us for this holiday period are both under-18 so they can't handle alcohol alone, don't schedule either of them unless there is at least one adult working at the same time. Maria has a family event on Friday, so don't schedule her any shifts that day, and on Sundays, she needs to finish before midnight because buses don't run late. Ben goes to university so can't do shifts starting at 16:00 on the weekdays, 17:00 and after is okay. 

Don't schedule FT staff to work more than 5 days in total, and PT shouldn't work more than 4 days in total, this is in their contracts. I want to be a good employer, so I want the PTers to have at least 2 consecutive days off (including our closed Wednesday), it would be annoying if they had to come in to work every other day. I need the total hours for each employee for this week to calculate payroll, FT are on £16.5 per hour, Nate and Jack who are only with us for this seasonal rush are on £14 per hour, Ben and Finn who are our regular PTers are on £14.5 per hour, sum up each employee's total hours at the end.

prompts.prompt_text:
1 week rota for my employees for 15th-21st December 2025, I have 2 FT (26-34 hour per week) and 4 PT employees (16-24 hours per week). Full-time employees are Maria and Nuria, part-time employees are Nate, Jack, Ben, and Finn. We are a bar closing at late times so the shifts are 16:00-22:00, 16:00-23:00, 18:00-01:00, 19:00-01:00, 1 person per shift for Thursday-Sunday inclusive. Monday-Tuesday shifts are 16:00-21:00, 16:00-23:00, 17:00-23:00. We are closed on Wednesdays. It's coming up to Christmas holiday season so I'm having trouble making this rota around my employees booked days off. Can you make this rota? 

Full-time employees are also senior staff, so I need at least one FTer to work the closing shift to cash-up every night we are open (the PTers aren't trained to do this). Also, Nate and Jack who joined us for this holiday period are both under-18 so they can't handle alcohol alone, don't schedule either of them unless there is at least one adult working at the same time. Maria has a family event on Friday, so don't schedule her any shifts that day, and on Sundays, she needs to finish before midnight because buses don't run late. Ben goes to university so can't do shifts starting at 16:00 on the weekdays, 17:00 and after is okay. 

Don't schedule FT staff to work more than 5 days in total, and PT shouldn't work more than 4 days in total, this is in their contracts. I want to be a good employer, so I want the PTers to have at least 2 consecutive days off (including our closed Wednesday), it would be annoying if they had to come in to work every other day. I need the total hours for each employee for this week to calculate payroll, FT are on £16.5 per hour, Nate and Jack who are only with us for this seasonal rush are on £14 per hour, Ben and Finn who are our regular PTers are on £14.5 per hour, sum up each employee's total hours at the end.

taxonomy.label: Never surfaced in reasoning
taxonomy.description: The requirement appears nowhere in the reasoning trace or the answer — it was never extracted from the prompt into the model's working plan (e.g., a formatting sub-rule the planning checklist skips entirely).
taxonomy.training_implication: Constraint-extraction SFT: reward exhaustive requirement enumeration before drafting; checklist-style supervision.

taxonomy.label: Tracked in reasoning, lost from answer
taxonomy.description: The trace tracks or even verifies the requirement, but iterative replanning, patchwork corrections, or final transcription loses it — the answer omits or contradicts what the trace established.
taxonomy.training_implication: CoT→answer faithfulness rewards: penalize final answers that drop or contradict constraints their own trace satisfied; long-horizon state tracking across plan revisions.

taxonomy.label: Noticed, then overridden
taxonomy.description: The trace names the constraint, then argues itself out of honoring it — habit, source-material conventions, helpfulness instincts, or a self-invented reinterpretation wins over the explicit instruction.
taxonomy.training_implication: Instruction-priority preference data: explicit user constraints must outrank priors, source formatting, and the model's own style habits.

taxonomy.label: Sacrificed to a competing constraint
taxonomy.description: Under real or perceived conflict (coverage vs ceilings, word caps vs completeness, time budget vs task list), the model satisfies one requirement by violating another — often asserting compliance anyway instead of surfacing the tradeoff.
taxonomy.training_implication: Preference data over constraint conflicts: teach surfacing and arbitrating conflicts — or flagging infeasibility — instead of silently sacrificing and overclaiming.

taxonomy.label: Constraint misread
taxonomy.description: The requirement is engaged with but interpreted wrongly — scope, boundary semantics ('every week after', 'even if zero'), conditional triggers, or format words ('brackets', 'beside') resolved to the wrong reading.
taxonomy.training_implication: Contrastive instruction-semantics SFT on scope/boundary/conditional phrasings with minimal pairs.

taxonomy.label: Source data misread
taxonomy.description: The failure originates in parsing the prompt's source material: column misalignment, false equivalences between sections, ambiguity silently resolved in the wrong direction.
taxonomy.training_implication: Structured-input robustness data (tables, rosters, misaligned columns) with explicit field re-derivation before use; largely auto-checkable, so RLVR-ready.

taxonomy.label: Right intent, wrong execution
taxonomy.description: The plan is right but the rendering fails: arithmetic/counting errors, format markup omitted, per-item rules replaced by one template, placeholders never resolved, output never cross-checked against its own derived values.
taxonomy.training_implication: Verifier-based RL: these criteria are mostly auto-checkable (counts, formats, arithmetic) — reward outputs that pass mechanical validators plus a final self-check pass.

taxonomy.label: Degenerate generation
taxonomy.description: The generation collapses — repetition loops, endless self-correction, no committed final answer — so whole constraint blocks go unmet at once.
taxonomy.training_implication: Decoding/termination training: penalize non-terminating self-correction loops; reward committing to a finalized answer within budget.

taxonomy.label: Constraint unaddressed (no trace)
taxonomy.description: The answer neither satisfies nor engages the constraint; without a reasoning trace, extraction misses and synthesis drops cannot be told apart.
taxonomy.training_implication: Coarse signal only — rerun with reasoning enabled to split extraction vs synthesis.

taxonomy.label: Judge suspect
taxonomy.description: You cannot independently locate the asserted failure: reading the response (and trace, if present) the criterion appears satisfied. Use this instead of inventing a root cause.
taxonomy.training_implication: None — candidate for judge error; feeds the human-validation priority queue.

taxonomy.label: Other
taxonomy.description: A real failure that fits none of the categories above. Describe it precisely in `rationale`.
taxonomy.training_implication: Unclassified — a rising rate here means the taxonomy needs revision.

comparison: Configs differ on three axes (limit 3 vs 20, reasoning off vs on, sample_seed null vs fixed 20260706), so E06 and E05 are different samples AND different treatments — all comparison here is directional and confounded, not a like-for-like delta.

Directionally, execution_slip jumped to the clear #1 in E06 (38/72 ≈ 53%) versus #3 in E05 (30/219 ≈ 14%); with reasoning disabled and only n=3, this could be a real reasoning-off effect or pure small-sample noise — cannot separate them.

Five E05 categories (constraint_dropped #1, constraint_overridden, constraint_never_surfaced, judge_suspect, other) are entirely absent in E06; at n=3 with 72 diagnosed criteria this is expected sparsity, not evidence they were resolved.
degenerate_output held at 15 but migrated model: 100% qwen-9b in E05 → 14/15 qwen-35b in E06. A cause that swaps its host model across runs is an anomaly, not a stable model-scale signature.
constraint_misread stayed present and mid-pack in both (35→10), the only cause with roughly consistent relative standing across the two runs.
prior_recommendations_review: Rec 1 (robustness, re-run identical config at limit>=60 with fixed seed): NOT addressed — E06 went the opposite direction to limit=3 and also changed the reasoning flag, making the Pareto even harder to trust rather than stabilizing it.
Rec 2 (judge_reliability, human-score ~40 items on top three causes): NOT addressed — no validation run present; the taxonomy boundaries remain unverified.

Rec 3 (discrepancy_drill, degenerate_output reasoning=true vs false on the 15 qwen-9b items): PARTIALLY addressed — E06 flipped reasoning to false globally, but not as a controlled A/B on those items; the result (degenerate_output moving to qwen-35b) muddies rather than resolves the question.

recommendations.action: Run limit>=60 at ONE frozen config (pick reasoning=false, temp=0.6 to match E06's treatment) with a fixed sample_seed, and report by_root_cause shares with confidence intervals.
recommendations.rationale: The program has never produced two adequately-sized runs at the same config; n=3 (E06) and a different-treatment n=20 (E05) cannot establish a Pareto, and the top cause has reshuffled every time. This is the prerequisite that both prior and current data lack.
recommendations.expected_signal: If execution_slip remains #1 with a stable share and the next 2-3 causes hold order, the Pareto is real; if ranking reshuffles again, failures are still noise-limited and config-sensitive.

recommendations.action: Take a fixed set of the same prompts and score degenerate_output under reasoning=true vs reasoning=false at temp=0.6, holding model and seed constant, tracking which model produces it.
recommendations.rationale: degenerate_output changed host model between runs (qwen-9b→qwen-35b) exactly when reasoning was toggled — a controlled A/B is the only way to tell a capability floor from a decoding/config artifact, and it was only half-done in E06.
recommendations.expected_signal: If degenerate_output tracks the reasoning flag it is a mechanical config issue to remove from the taxonomy; if it persists per-model regardless, it is a genuine per-model mode to characterize.

recommendations.action: Human/census-score a stratified ~40-item subset covering execution_slip, constraint_misread, and constraint_sacrificed for classifier agreement, using the frozen classifier_prompt_sha256 88d130c223aa.
recommendations.rationale: These causes now drive the ranking but have never been human-validated across two experiments; execution_slip's sudden dominance could partly reflect the classifier absorbing other categories when reasoning traces disappear.
recommendations.expected_signal: High agreement lets a future intervention trust the top causes; low agreement means taxonomy boundaries must be tightened before any training decision.

synthesis.iteration_note: Early and unstable on the iterate-vs-train curve. Despite two experiments, no two runs share a config and the top cause has changed each time, so the Pareto is not yet established — intervention_ready is premature. The immediate need is one adequately-powered, frozen-config run before this program can converge.
